sentences.text: What if the famous knight of faith in this engraving was never a hero?
This is Knight, Death and the Devil, engraved by Albrecht Dürer in 1513.
For centuries, the rider has been read as a Christian soldier protected by the armour of his faith.
Nietzsche even gave a print to Wagner as a symbol of a brave future.
And the picture seems to agree.
The knight stares ahead while Death and the Devil crowd beside his horse.
A fox tail hangs from its tip.
According to the writers Sten Karling and Ursula Meyer, the work did not seek to glorify the knight.
In early Christian symbolism, the fox stood for greed, cunning and treachery.
And Dorothy Getlein saw his face as resigned and downcast.
He isn't a hero of faith.
He's a resigned rider with Death as his companion.
So is he a saint in armour, or a man who already gave up?

meta.title: Everyone Called Him a Hero... Then They Saw the FOX Tail #history #art
meta.description: Knight, Death and the Devil is an engraving by Albrecht Dürer from 1513. It is usually read as a Christian knight protected by his faith, but Sten Karling and Ursula Meyer argued it did not glorify him: a fox tail, a symbol of greed and cunning, hangs from his lance.
meta.question: A saint in armour, or a man who gave up?
